content: Aluminium phosphate (AlPO4) is a chemical compound. Its anhydrous form naturally occurs as the mineral berlinite. Various synthetic forms of anhydrous aluminium phosphate exist, many of which have framework structures similar to zeolites. Some of these synthetic forms are utilized as catalysts or molecular sieves. The dihydrate form, AlPO4·2H2O, is found in nature as the minerals variscite and meta-variscite. A pentahydrate form (AlPO4·5H2O) is also known. Commercially, aluminium phosphate is available as a gel. Aluminium phosphate (berlinite) is isoelectronic with silicon dioxide (SiO2). Berlinite resembles quartz in appearance and has a similar structure, with silicon atoms replaced by aluminium and phosphorus atoms. The structure alternates between AlO4 and PO4 tetrahedra. Like quartz, AlPO4 exhibits chirality and piezoelectric properties. When crystalline berlinite is heated, it transforms into tridymite and cristobalite forms, mirroring the behavior of silicon dioxide. The dihydrate form of aluminium phosphate, found as variscite and meta-variscite, consists of a structural assembly of phosphate anions, aluminium cations, and water molecules. The aluminium cations in this structure are six-coordinate. Aluminium phosphate molecular sieves, generically referred to as ALPOs, were first reported in 1982. These materials share the same chemical composition (AlPO4) and possess framework structures with microporous cavities. The frameworks are composed of alternating AlO4 and PO4 tetrahedra. The denser, cavity-less crystalline form of AlPO4, berlinite, also features this alternating tetrahedral structure. The framework structures of aluminophosphate molecular sieves differ in the orientation of the AlO4 and PO4 tetrahedra, resulting in cavities of varying sizes. In this respect, they are similar to aluminosilicate zeolites, although zeolites have electrically charged frameworks. A typical preparation of aluminophosphate involves the hydrothermal reaction of phosphoric acid with aluminium in the form of hydroxide, an aluminium salt (e.g., aluminium nitrate), or alkoxide under controlled pH conditions in the presence of organic amines. These organic molecules act as templates, now referred to as structure-directing agents (SDAs), guiding the growth of the porous framework. In medicine, aluminium phosphate sol is used as an adsorbent for toxoids. In its dried form, which contains hydrated AlPO4, it is employed as an antacid. Industrially, the Al-PO4-H2O system serves as the basis for various adhesives, binders, and cements. Naturally occurring aluminium phosphate is unstable when exposed to heat. However, in geologically stable regions such as Australia and Southern Africa, aluminium phosphate is often the predominant form of phosphorus in soils. It forms when phosphate in rainwater reacts with dissolved aluminium in the soil. Although not as insoluble as many other soil components in these regions, aluminium phosphate can form highly insoluble double salts known as taranakites. These salts incorporate essential elements for plant growth, such as potassium and nitrogen, which are typically highly soluble in water. In coastal areas of South Africa and Namibia, the combination of ancient soils and a high input of phosphate from nutrient-rich ocean waters, driven by the Benguela Current, leads to the accumulation of aluminium phosphate as a concentrated mineral known as aluminium phosphate rock. Interest in mining these deposits as a source of phosphorus for agriculture has only emerged in recent years. If low-cost treatment methods become feasible, these deposits could hold significant economic value.
